Word Vector Geometry.script:
Most students think once you’ve trained Word2Vec, “similarity” is a solved problem. But your embeddings’ geometry can quietly wreck your nearest neighbors and search results if you’re not paying attention to it.

You’ve already learned that Word2Vec learns dense word and context vectors, and that it uses their dot product inside a softmax to model similarity and predict context words. That’s a solid foundation, but there are some important geometric details your course didn’t cover that really matter once you start using these vectors for search, recommendation, or any real retrieval system.

Let’s start with cosine versus dot product. The dot product between two word vectors mixes two things: how aligned their directions are, and how long each vector is. Cosine similarity divides by the lengths, so it keeps only the angle, the pure directional match. The key insight here is that in trained embeddings, vector length isn’t random: norms usually grow with word frequency. So if you rank neighbors by raw dot product, you’re often rewarding “popular” high‑frequency words rather than the most semantically similar ones. If you’re looking at the slide, you can see the comparison diagram: the query vector in the middle, one big‑norm frequent candidate, one small‑norm rare candidate. Dot‑product ranking tends to favor the big one, even if its direction’s a bit off. Cosine ranking, by normalizing, tends to favor the one whose direction actually matches the query best. This is where it gets important: for semantic search, we usually care more about “which way the vector points” than how big it is, so teams often explicitly normalize to unit length or compute cosine for retrieval.

Now let’s shift to all‑but‑the‑top postprocessing. Real embedding spaces are often anisotropic: most vectors live in a narrow cone and share a few dominant directions that reflect very generic corpus patterns, not fine‑grained meaning. All‑but‑the‑top tries to fix that. If you’re looking at the process‑flow diagram, we start with the raw embeddings, then mean‑center them by subtracting the average vector. Next, we run PCA to find the directions that explain the most variance across the vocabulary. Finally, we subtract each vector’s projection on the top one to three principal components. The key idea is that you’re peeling off those “background” directions so the remaining space is more isotropic and local semantic differences stand out better. In practice, after this step, neighbors of a word like “motel” shift away from extremely frequent, generic words and toward things like “hotel” and “inn”.

Building on that, subword, or n‑gram, embeddings tackle a different geometric problem: rare and out‑of‑vocabulary words. Instead of giving each token its own standalone vector, you build a word vector by composing the vectors of its character n‑grams. On the slide’s concept map, you can see: start from the word token, break it into subword chunks, map those to n‑gram vectors, then sum or average them to get a composed embedding. Here’s what makes this different: now “motels” shares many n‑grams with “motel” and “hotel”, so even if “motels” is rare, its vector lands close to that semantic neighborhood. That improves geometry and nearest neighbors for low‑frequency and unseen forms in production systems.

Now, a lot of students walk away thinking dot product and cosine are basically interchangeable, and that they’ll give you the same nearest neighbors anyway. But here’s the thing: as soon as vector norms vary, especially with frequency, they really don’t. Dot product bakes in length, so high‑norm words can dominate your rankings. Cosine strips length out and focuses on direction, which often gives you neighbors that are actually more semantically related.

Before I wrap up, I want you to pause for a moment and think about this: if you took a trained Word2Vec model you’ve seen, and switched your neighbor search from raw dot product to cosine on normalized vectors, which words’ neighbors do you expect would change the most, and why?

So here’s what I want you to take away from this. First, dot product and cosine are not the same: norms matter, and cosine removes that length effect. Second, embedding spaces have dominant directions that can blur fine‑grained meaning, and all‑but‑the‑top postprocessing can sharpen your neighbors. Third, subword embeddings reshape geometry for rare and unseen tokens by sharing information across word forms. Once you understand and control this geometry, your embeddings become much more reliable tools in real systems.

Self-Attention Fundamentals.module_md:
## Module Overview
Imagine you are building a Transformer-based language model that must decide which previous words matter when predicting the next token — for example, resolving pronouns in a long sentence or aligning source/target phrases in translation. Self-attention Fundamentals provide the mechanism that lets each token compute queries, keys, and values, compare them pairwise, and form context-dependent weighted sums that drive those decisions. This topic matters now because attention is the core of Transformer models widely used in industry, and production systems require not only the basic math but also stable, efficient implementations (numerical stability, masking, projection shapes, and scaling). In this module you will learn those practical, production-minded additions beyond the course: how and why to use scaled dot-product attention, projection matrix shapes and reshaping for multi-heads, and implementation best-practices for masking and softmax stability. Ready to turn textbook attention into reliable, production-ready attention? 

## Learning Objectives
- Explain how queries (Q), keys (K), values (V), pairwise scores e_ij = q_i · k_j, softmax over j, and the weighted sum of V produce per-token attentive outputs (Curriculum)
- Implement scaled dot-product attention including the 1/sqrt(d_k) scaling and a numerically stable masked softmax for causal masking (Gap)
- Describe the shapes and roles of learned projection matrices W_Q, W_K, W_V, and W_O, and perform the per-head reshaping/concatenation required for multi-head attention (Gap)
- Apply masking, softmax-stabilization (subtract-max), and attention-dropout in a batched attention implementation and diagnose common shape/mask errors (Gap)
- Evaluate O(n^2) runtime/memory trade-offs for standard self-attention and compare when to consider sparse or low-rank approximations (Apply) (Gap)

## Curriculum Coverage
The curriculum teaches self-attention as the foundational mechanism for Transformer models. It presents the per-token construction of queries, keys, and values and shows how attention computes all pairwise dot products to produce attention scores. The matrix form is emphasized: given input X (n × d), linear projections produce XQ, XK, XV, and attention is computed by matrix-multiplying queries with keys' transpose to get an n × n score matrix, applying softmax across each query's row, and using that to weight values and produce an output of shape n × d.

Multi-head attention is covered: separate Q, K, V projection matrices for each head (Q_l, K_l, V_l) produce independent attention outputs which are concatenated and mixed with an output projection Y. The curriculum also treats necessities around self-attention: positional representations (to encode order because attention is permutation-invariant), masking (to prevent peeking at future tokens during parallelized computation), and the addition of nonlinearities via a post-attention feed-forward network to give depth beyond pure weighted averages. Practical matrix-flow explanations (sequence-stacked form) are included to connect per-token math to batched matrix operations.

Before continuing, make sure you can answer:
- What are the three per-token vectors used in self-attention and how are attention scores computed from them?
- How is multi-head attention constructed from single-head attention computations?
- Why are positional representations required in self-attention architectures?

## Identified Gaps
The curriculum gives a solid theoretical and matrix-level grounding in self-attention, but industry demands additional, practical knowledge to implement and operate attention at scale. Missing or underdeveloped areas include: the scaled dot-product detail (the 1/sqrt(d_k) factor) and numerical-stability practices for softmax, concrete shapes and learned projection matrices with per-head dimensioning and reshaping rules, masked/causal softmax broadcasting and attention-dropout, and awareness of runtime/memory scaling plus common efficient alternatives. These are opportunities: mastering them increases employability for engineering roles that implement or optimize Transformers and reduces time lost troubleshooting training instabilities and mask bugs.

Priorities:
- Scaled dot-product and numerical-stability practices: (Critical) — fundamental to stable training and ubiquitous in production.
- Projection matrix shapes, per-head reshaping, and correct mask application: (Critical) — frequent source of implementation bugs and needed for multi-head implementations.
- O(n^2) complexity awareness and familiarity with efficient/approximate attention variants: (Important) — crucial when working with long contexts or tight memory budgets.
- Diagnostic and interpretability practices (head pruning, visualization caveats): (Important/Nice-to-have) — valuable for model analysis and optimization, but secondary to getting attention to run reliably.

## Core Content

### What You Need to Learn
Top gaps to close: (1) Scaled dot-product attention and numerical stability; (2) Learned projection matrices, per-head shapes, masking, and correct batched implementation.

Gap 1 — Scaled dot-product attention and numerical-stability
- Building on what you studied about e_ij = q_i · k_j and softmax, scaled dot-product attention modifies the raw scores before softmax to keep logits in a numerically well-behaved range. Definition: scaled dot-product attention divides query-key dot products by sqrt(d_k) (the per-head key dimensionality) before applying softmax; this prevents the dot products from growing with dimension and producing extremely peaked/flat softmax outputs that harm gradients.
- How it works (walkthrough):
  1. Compute Q_head and K_head where each has dimension d_k (after projection and reshaping).
  2. Compute scores S = Q_head × K_head^T (shape: n_q × n_k).
  3. Scale: S_scaled = S / sqrt(d_k).
  4. (Optional) For causal masking, set masked positions to a large negative value (see Gap 2 for broadcasting/masking).
  5. For numerical stability, subtract the row-wise maximum from S_scaled before exponentiating: S_shifted = S_scaled − max_row(S_scaled).
  6. Apply softmax across each row to get attention weights A.
  7. Optionally apply attention-dropout to A.
  8. Output = A × V_head.
- Practical example from industry practice: In production Transformer implementations (e.g., the original Transformer design), attention uses 1/sqrt(d_k) scaling; implementers also subtract the row maximum before softmax to avoid overflow/underflow, and they apply attention-dropout on the normalized weights during training to regularize attention patterns.

Gap 2 — Projection matrices, head shapes, masking, and batched implementation
- Building on the curriculum matrix-view of XQ, XK, XV, we now define the learned projection matrices and the per-head reshape/concat steps. Definition: W_Q, W_K, W_V ∈ R^{d_model × d_model} (or separate per-head blocks) are learned linear projections that map input vectors to query/key/value spaces; for h heads, each head uses d_k = d_model / h (commonly) so that after projection you reshape the (n × d_model) projected tensor into (n × h × d_k), transpose to (h × n × d_k) to treat heads as a batch, compute attention per head, then concatenate head outputs and apply an output projection W_O ∈ R^{d_model × d_model}.
- How it works (step-by-step implementation checklist):
  1. Given input X of shape (batch, n, d_model), compute Q = X × W_Q, K = X × W_K, V = X × W_V producing (batch, n, d_model) each.
  2. Reshape each to (batch, n, h, d_k) and transpose to (batch, h, n, d_k) or (batch*h, n, d_k) depending on framework; this lets you compute attention for all heads in parallel.
  3. For each head, compute S = Q × K^T → shape (batch, h, n, n), scale by 1/sqrt(d_k).
  4. Apply masks (padding or causal). Masks must broadcast to (batch, h, n, n) or be unsqueezed appropriately; masked entries are set to -inf (or a large negative) before softmax.
  5. Apply numerical-stable softmax (subtract max per row), attention-dropout, then multiply by V to get per-head outputs (batch, h, n, d_k).
  6. Concatenate heads back to (batch, n, d_model) and apply W_O to mix head outputs.
- Concrete industry-practice notes: implementers often treat the head axis as a batch dimension for efficient GEMM operations, ensure masks are broadcast-compatible (e.g., expand dims to match head count), and use attention-dropout on the weight matrix A. Unit tests typically check shapes after each reshape and verify that masked positions receive zero total attention in causal settings.

Lesser gaps (brief summaries)
- O(n^2) complexity and efficient alternatives: standard self-attention is quadratic in sequence length and memory; when handling long contexts, engineers consider sparse/local attention (Longformer/BigBird), low-rank or kernelized approximations (Linformer, Performer), or Nyström approximations — each trades accuracy, memory, and speed differently. Learn more from the referenced papers in Further Reading.
- Interpretability caveats and diagnostics: attention weights are useful diagnostics but not definitive explanations; head pruning and visualization are practical tools—see Further Reading.

### Common Misconceptions
- Misconception: "You can omit the 1/sqrt(d_k) scaling without consequence."  
  Why it's wrong: Without scaling, dot-product magnitudes grow with d_k, making softmax inputs large and potentially causing vanishing gradients or overly sharp distributions.  
  Correct understanding: Always scale by 1/sqrt(d_k) (or equivalent temperature tuning) to stabilize softmax behavior across different head sizes.

- Misconception: "Masking is simply an elementwise multiply after softmax."  
  Why it's wrong: Multiplying by zero after softmax does not prevent future information from influencing softmax normalization; masks must be applied to logits (e.g., set logits to -inf or a large negative) before softmax so masked positions do not contribute to normalization.  
  Correct understanding: Apply masks to the scaled logits with correct broadcasting, then apply a numerically-stable softmax.

- Misconception: "Attention weights equal interpretability explanations."  
  Why it's wrong: Attention shows how the model distributes weight given its representations, but weights alone do not establish causal attribution for model decisions.  
  Correct understanding: Use attention as one diagnostic among others (probing, ablation, head pruning) and be cautious interpreting it as explanation.

## Industry Context
Roles that value these skills include: (1) NLP/ML Engineer implementing Transformer models for production inference and training, (2) Research Engineer or Applied Scientist working on model architecture or efficiency improvements, and (3) ML Infrastructure Engineer optimizing batched attention performance and memory usage. Employers expect familiarity with both the mathematical core of attention and implementation practices that keep models numerically stable and efficient.

Real-world use case (detailed): A machine-translation service uses a Transformer encoder-decoder. The encoder produces contextual representations of a source sentence; the decoder uses cross-attention (queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder outputs) to focus on relevant source positions when generating each target token. In production, the team must implement scaled dot-product attention with causal masking and attention-dropout, ensure projection matrix shapes and reshaping steps are correct for multi-head attention, and profile attention O(n^2) memory usage to decide maximum input sizes or whether to adopt sparse attention for long documents. The outcome: stable, high-quality translations with predictable latency and memory behavior.

What employers look for: practical implementation experience with Q/K/V projections and multi-head reshaping, demonstrated understanding of scaling and numerical-stability fixes, experience applying masks correctly in batched contexts, and familiarity with trade-offs of efficient/approximate attention methods when deploying models to handle long sequences.

## Practice & Review

### Quick Check
1. What are the three vectors computed per token in self-attention and how is a single attention score e_ij formed?  
> Answer: Queries (Q), Keys (K), Values (V); e_ij = q_i · k_j (dot product).

2. In multi-head attention, after projecting inputs to Q, K, V, how are head outputs combined to produce the final output?  
> Answer: Each head computes attention independently on its d_k-dimensional slices; head outputs are concatenated and then multiplied by an output projection W_O.

3. Why is scaling by 1/sqrt(d_k) applied before softmax, and what numerical trick further stabilizes softmax computation?  
> Answer: Scaling prevents dot products from growing with d_k and producing extreme softmax logits; further stability is gained by subtracting the row-wise maximum from logits before softmax.

4. You must implement causal masked attention for a batched input with h heads. Describe one potential broadcasting pitfall and how to avoid it.  
> Answer: Pitfall: applying a (batch, n, n) mask to a (batch, h, n, n) logits tensor without expanding the head dimension leads to shape mismatch or incorrect broadcasting; avoid by unsqueezing/expanding mask to (batch, 1, n, n) or (batch, h, n, n) before applying.

### Apply It
Scenario: You are adding a new self-attention layer to a Transformer training pipeline. Training diverges on large batch sizes and the attention logits appear to saturate; furthermore, a unit test reveals that causal masking sometimes fails and the model peeks at future tokens. Your task is to fix the attention layer so training is stable and masking is correct.

Tasks:
- Inspect and correct the Q/K projection shapes and the per-head reshaping code; add assertions or unit tests for expected shapes at each step.
- Add the 1/sqrt(d_k) scaling and implement a row-wise subtract-max before softmax; apply attention-dropout during training.
- Fix mask application by ensuring masks are applied to logits with correct broadcasting (setting masked logits to a large negative value) before softmax.
- Run a short training experiment to verify stability and that causal positions receive zero attention to future tokens.

Expected outcome/deliverable: A patched attention implementation with tests verifying shape correctness and masking, logs showing reduced softmax saturation and stable training loss over initial steps, and a short report summarizing the fixes and their effects.

Self-Attention Fundamentals.script:
Imagine you’re on your first day as an ML engineer, and your brand‑new Transformer keeps blowing up in training… even though the attention math looks exactly like what you learned in class. What’s actually going wrong?

You’ve already learned about queries, keys, values, eᵢⱼ = qᵢ · kⱼ, softmax over keys, and the multi‑head matrix form of attention. That’s a solid foundation, but production models need extra details to stay numerically stable, handle shapes correctly, and scale to long sequences. Let’s close those gaps so your mental picture of attention matches what real code is doing.

First, scaled dot‑product and stability. In theory you can just take QKᵀ, softmax, then multiply by V. In practice, that breaks once dₖ gets big. The key insight is that dot products grow with dimension, so the logits going into softmax become huge, the distribution gets extremely peaked, and gradients basically vanish. To fix this, production attention divides the score matrix S = QKᵀ by √dₖ, per head. With dₖ = 128, you’re dividing every logit by about 11.3, which keeps them in a reasonable range.

This is where it gets important: you also need a numerically stable softmax. You add your mask as a giant negative number, like −1e9, to disallowed positions, then subtract the row‑wise maximum before exponentiating. That “subtract max” doesn’t change the softmax result, but it prevents overflow. If you’re looking at the process‑flow diagram, this is the “Scale & Mask” box, then “Subtract Max,” then softmax to get A, apply dropout on A, and finally A @ V to get the output. For a causal mask, all future tokens in a row get −1e9, so after softmax they get essentially zero attention.

Now let’s shift to projection shapes and reshaping. You already know there are multiple heads; the tricky part is keeping the tensor shapes straight. The key idea: every reshape must preserve total dimension D. Start with X of shape (B, N, D). You project once per type: Q = X W_Q, K = X W_K, V = X W_V, all still (B, N, D). Then you reshape each to (B, N, h, dₖ) where h is heads and dₖ = D / h, and permute to (B, h, N, dₖ). Now each head acts like its own mini‑batch.

Per head you compute S = QKᵀ with shape (B, h, N, N), apply the same scaling, masking, subtract‑max, and softmax, then A @ V gives you (B, h, N, dₖ). Finally, you re‑permute back to (B, N, h, dₖ), reshape to (B, N, D), and apply W_O. If you’re looking at the concept‑map diagram, you can see that flow: X, then W_Q/K/V, reshape to heads, per‑head attention, then concat and W_O. Most real‑world bugs in attention come from messing up one of those reshapes or forgetting to broadcast the mask to (B, h, N, N), so engineers write unit tests specifically for these shape and mask edge cases.

Finally, attention scaling and alternatives. Standard attention builds an N×N score matrix per head, which means O(N²) time and memory. For long sequences, that blows up. So industry models often swap in approximate schemes: sparse local windows, a mix of local plus a few global tokens, or low‑rank and kernelized variants that make attention closer to O(N). The trade‑off is less exact attention but feasible long‑context inference.

Now, a lot of students think the brighter a cell is on an attention heatmap, the more that token is “the reason” for the model’s prediction. But attention weights aren’t guaranteed causal explanations; they’re just one view of how information’s being routed given the current representations. In practice, people treat them as diagnostics and combine them with ablations or probing, not as proof of why the model decided something.

Before I wrap up, pause for a moment and see if you can mentally walk through the full production attention pipeline: from X, to Q/K/V, to per‑head reshape, to scaled and masked logits, to softmax, to A @ V, and back through W_O.

So here’s what I want you to take away from this. First, always scale QKᵀ by 1/√dₖ and subtract the row‑wise max before softmax to keep training stable. Second, get very comfortable with the shapes: X, Q/K/V, per‑head reshapes, and mask broadcasting. Third, remember that dense attention is O(N²), so real systems often use sparse or low‑rank tricks for long contexts. And finally, treat attention maps as helpful clues, not definitive explanations. With these pieces in place, you’re much closer to writing attention that actually works in production.
